Gender and Technology in Urban Space: A Study of the Smart Cities of Bhubaneswar and New Delhi

Abstract:

The notion of the Smart City reflects a concrete manifestation of techno-urbanism narrative. Launched in 2015, the Government of India&rsquos Smart Cities Mission sought to enhance infrastructure, sustainability, and social inclusiveness across 100 cities via digital technology. By placing a premium on IT, private capital, inclusion, and community participation, the mission marks a distinct postmodern turn in postcolonial urban planning. However, urban transformations inevitably alter gendered spatial relations. Grounded in Feminist Technology Studies (FTS) and a postmodern urbanism framework, this thesis critically evaluates whether technology-led transformations synthesize efficiency with equity to honour the &lsquoRight to the City,&rsquo or inadvertently reproduce socio-spatial and digital exclusions. This empirical comparative research investigates the dialectical interface between gender, technology, and urban space in two socio-culturally distinct Indian cities &ndash Bhubaneswar and NDMC (New Delhi). Evaluating key sectors&mdashincluding transport, safety, housing, governance, education, health, water, and sanitation&mdashthe study assesses smart interventions across an analytical matrix of Availability, Accessibility, and Usability. It captures the everyday lived realities of citizens across intersectional categories of class (slum and non-slum), sexuality (transgender communities), and occupation (informal market vendors) as they navigate transformed residential, public, and commercial spaces. The empirical findings reveal a severe structural paradox &ndash high-tech deployments do not automatically enhance human capabilities or material security for vulnerable populations. Crucially, Bhubaneswar and NDMC display starkly contrasting trajectories of gendered spatial citizenship. In Bhubaneswar, progressive state-led initiatives like the JAGA Mission, Sweekruti, and MUKTA&mdashsupported by multilateral agencies and NGOs&mdashinstitutionalize a gendered Right to the City by formalizing land rights, upgrading informal settlements, and empowering transgender collectives as active municipal partners. Conversely, NDMC reflects a top-down, technocratic model where gender-friendly technological interventions remain conspicuous by their absence. Instead, tech-driven strategies enforce spatial purification and digital surveillance to serve elite consumption, decoupling vulnerable populations from spatial rights and digital welfare. Ultimately, the thesis demonstrates that true urban smartness requires a radical re-coding of data urbanism around intersectional care, labour dignity, and democratic sovereignty.

Keywords: Urban Space, Gender, Technology, Smart City, Bhubaneswar, NDMC (New Delhi).
